response.evidence: Analysis of loan outcomes by race shows 10 applications denied among 61 Black or African American applicants (16.4% denial rate) versus 119 denials among 1,121 total applicants (10.6% overall denial rate). While the denial rate for Black applicants appears elevated, the small sample size (n=61) and absence of controls for legitimate lending factors (debt-to-income ratio, loan-to-value ratio, credit metrics, etc.) prevents drawing reliable conclusions about discrimination. Comparative analysis across all racial groups and detailed statistical testing would be required for evidence-based conclusions.

While the dataset shows 1 denied loan among Black or African American applicants (1 denied, 4 originated = 20% denial rate), compared to an overall denial rate of approximately 7.5%, this small sample size (n=5) is insufficient for reliable statistical inference. The applicant's specific financial metrics (debt-to-income ratio, loan-to-value ratio, income, credit profile) are not provided, making it impossible to determine whether denial was based on protected class status or legitimate underwriting criteria. A rigorous discrimination analysis would require: (1) larger sample sizes, (2) applicant-level financial data, (3) matched comparison groups, and (4) multivariate analysis controlling for legitimate lending factors.

Analysis of the data shows no clear pattern of discrimination against non-Hispanic Black or African American males in the 35-44 age group. Among applicants matching your demographic profile (Non-Hispanic Black or African American male, age 35-44), the approval rate is approximately 87% (13 originations vs 2 denials out of 15 total applications). This rate is comparable to or better than approval rates for other demographic groups in the dataset. Loan denials appear to be driven by standard underwriting factors (debt-to-income ratios, loan amounts, property values, income levels) rather than race/ethnicity. Without access to rejected applications from other groups with identical financial profiles, a definitive discrimination conclusion cannot be made from this data alone.
